previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of cocaine-induced cardiomyopathy, systolic heart failure, COPD, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Initial concern for pulmonary embolism was ruled out with a negative D-dimer and VQ scan, and lower extremity ultrasound showed no DVT. The chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, likely from coughing, and resolved during the admission. He was found to be fluid-overloaded, with weight above his dry weight and mild pulmonary edema, prompting IV diuresis. He was transitioned back to home torsemide with the addition of weekly metolazone. Losartan was reduced to 12.5 mg daily due to kidney concerns. His troponin elevation was attributed to chronic heart and kidney disease. He remained stable, with improved volume status and resolution of symptoms, and was discharged home with follow-up for a lung nodule and iron deficiency anemia.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___, 

It was a pleasure to take care of you during your 
hospitalization at ___. You came to the hospital because you 
were having difficulty breathing and episodes of passing out. 
You were found to have some fluid in your lungs due to your 
heart failure and we gave you IV diuretics and you improved. 
Your kidney function also improved with diuresis and you were at 
your dry weight prior to discharge. Please make sure to eat a 
low salt diet, take your medications, weigh yourself every 
morning, and call MD if weight goes up more than 3 lbs.

We did a work up to determine what caused you to pass out and 
your head CT, ekg, telemetry, lab tests were normal. You were 
seen by neurology who did not feel these were due to seizures. 
It is likely these occurred from coughing which is not uncommon. 
We had the pulmonology team see you and they recommended follow 
up as an outpatient to optimize your lung function. 

Please continue to take the rest of your medications as 
prescribed and attend all follow up appointments as listed 
below. If you develop a recurrence of the same symptoms that 
originally brought you to the hospital, experience any of the 
warning signs below, or have any other symptoms that concern 
you, please seek medical attention. Best of luck to you in your 
future health. 

It was a pleasure taking care of you!
Your ___ Care Team

CT THORAX: The thyroid gland is normal. Massive mediastinal lymphadenopathy is
not significantly changed in the prevascular, peritracheal and subcarinal
stations. The largest lymph node continues to measure up to 4 cm in size in
the anterior mediastinum (02:33). The thoracic aorta is normal in caliber. The
pulmonary artery remains dilated, measuring 33 mm in diameter (02:41)
suggesting underlying pulmonary hypertension. The heart is moderately enlarged
with a small pericardial effusion. Coronary artery calcifications are diffuse.

A spiculated pulmonary nodule in the right upper lobe (4:137) measuring 13 x
12 mm is not significantly changed in size or morphology.  No other suspicious
lesions are identified. Within the pulmonary parenchyma, there is unchanged
extensive fat mosaic attenuation pattern of the lungs with areas of relatively
decreased vascularity and disparity between the size of the pulmonary arteries
at the same level (for example, in the right lower lobe 4:184) suggestive of
chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease. There is no pleural effusion, focal
consolidation or pneumothorax.

There is a small hiatal hernia. Although this study is not tailored for the
evaluation of subdiaphragmatic contents, the imaged upper abdomen demonstrates
punctate density in the left kidney (2:79), which may represent a tiny
calculus.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES:  There are no osseous destructive lesions concerning for
malignancy.

chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease.

malignancy.
4.  Unchanged massive central thoracic lymphadenopathy.
5. Diffuse coronary atherosclerosis and moderate cardiomegaly.
